q: Which river flows through the center of Paris?
fact: The Seine runs about 777 km from Burgundy to the English Channel, and Paris has 37 bridges across it.

q: Which Italian city is famous for its canals, gondolas and Saint Mark's Square?
fact: Its gondolas are all painted black, and each one is slightly lopsided so the gondolier can steer with a single oar.

q: Which Paris landmark was the tallest structure in the world from 1889 until 1930?
fact: It was only meant to stand for 20 years, but it proved useful as a radio antenna and was kept.

q: What is the world's most visited art museum, home of the Mona Lisa?
fact: Its glass pyramid entrance, designed by the architect I. M. Pei, opened in 1989.

q: What is the title of France's national anthem?
fact: It was written in Strasbourg in 1792, but took its name from volunteers from Marseille who sang it as they marched into Paris.

q: What is the name of the Paris stadium where the French Open tennis tournament is played on red clay?
fact: It is named after a French pilot who made the first nonstop flight across the Mediterranean Sea, in 1913.

q: Which pyramid-shaped peak towers over the Swiss village of Zermatt?
fact: It is 4,478 m high and sits right on the border with Italy, where it is called Monte Cervino.

q: Which Swiss railway tunnel under the Alps, opened in 2016, is the longest in the world?
fact: It runs 57 km, and in places more than 2,000 m of rock lie above the trains.

q: Which cold Andalusian soup is blended from raw tomatoes, cucumber, peppers and garlic?
fact: It is a summer staple in southern Spain. Its thicker cousin from Cordoba, salmorejo, leaves out the cucumber and peppers.

q: Which Viennese composer, called 'the Waltz King', wrote The Blue Danube?
fact: The Blue Danube, from 1867, is played every year as an encore at the Vienna Philharmonic's New Year's Concert.

q: Which playwright from Stratford-upon-Avon wrote Romeo and Juliet and Hamlet?
fact: About 39 of his plays survive, and they have been translated into every major language.

q: Big Ben is really the name of the great bell. What is the official name of the London clock tower that holds it?
fact: It was simply called the Clock Tower until 2012, when it was renamed for Queen Elizabeth II's Diamond Jubilee.

q: Which small three-leaved plant is the best-known symbol of Ireland?
fact: Legend says Saint Patrick used it to explain the Holy Trinity. The official state emblem, though, is the harp.

q: Which Swedish furniture company is famous for flat-pack furniture you assemble yourself?
fact: Its blue and yellow logo matches the colors of the Swedish flag, and many of its products carry Swedish names.

q: Which paprika-spiced soup or stew is Hungary's best-known national dish?
fact: It was first cooked by cattle herders on the Hungarian plains - 'gulyas' means 'herdsman'.

q: Which mountain range is usually taken as the dividing line between the European and Asian parts of this country?
fact: The Urals run about 2,500 km from the Arctic coast down to Kazakhstan and are rich in minerals and gemstones.

q: What are the painted Russian wooden dolls that nest one inside another called?
fact: The first set, made in 1890, had eight dolls - the largest a girl holding a black rooster.

q: What is the name of the famous 200 km skating race through eleven towns of Friesland?
fact: It is held only when the ice is at least 15 cm thick along the whole route. The last one so far was in 1997.

q: Which Roman wall, begun in AD 122, ran right across northern England from coast to coast?
fact: It stretched about 117 km, with a small fort every Roman mile. Long sections can still be walked today.

q: Which German carmaker's name means 'people's car'?
fact: Its original Beetle was built for about 65 years, until 2003, and is one of the best-selling cars of all time.

q: Which arm of the Mediterranean lies between Italy and Croatia?
fact: Venice sits at its northern end, and Croatia's coast along it has more than 1,000 islands.

q: Which narrow strait separates southern Spain from Morocco?
fact: At its narrowest it is only about 14 km wide, linking the Atlantic Ocean with the Mediterranean Sea.

q: Which reindeer-herding people are native to the far north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia?
fact: Their homeland, Sapmi, crosses four borders, and Norway, Sweden and Finland each have an elected Sami parliament.

q: Which Renaissance genius painted the Mona Lisa?
fact: He also filled notebooks with designs for flying machines, many written in mirror-image script.

q: Which Norse god of thunder wields a hammer called Mjolnir?
fact: Thursday is named after him - it was 'Thor's day'.

q: Which currency, launched in 1999, is shared by most countries of the European Union?
fact: Its notes and coins arrived on January 1, 2002, replacing old currencies like the franc, the mark and the lira.

q: Which ancient Greek scientist from Syracuse is said to have shouted 'Eureka!' in his bath?
fact: He was working out whether a king's crown was pure gold by measuring how much water it pushed aside.

q: What is the name for the flag of Scotland, a white diagonal cross on a blue field?
fact: Its white X is also part of the Union Jack, where it sits behind the red crosses of England and Ireland.

q: Which German engineer built the first practical gasoline-powered car, patented in 1886?
fact: In 1888 his wife, Bertha, drove it about 100 km to visit her mother - the first long-distance car trip.

q: What is the name of Japan's highest mountain, an almost perfectly cone-shaped volcano?
fact: It stands 3,776 m high and last erupted in 1707.

q: What is the Japanese name for the country's high-speed 'bullet trains'?
fact: The fastest of them run at up to 320 km/h, and the network has carried billions of passengers since 1964.

q: What is the red disc on this flag meant to stand for?
fact: The flag is called Hinomaru, 'circle of the sun', and Japan's own name, Nihon, means 'origin of the sun'.

q: What is the name of Japan's national anthem, whose words come from a poem more than 1,000 years old?
fact: Its words were first written down in a poetry collection from the year 905, making them among the oldest of any anthem.

q: What is the name of the army of life-size clay soldiers found near Xi'an, China, in 1974?
fact: Farmers digging a well found it. There are thousands of soldiers, and no two faces are said to be exactly alike.

q: What is the longest river in this country, and in all of Asia?
fact: It runs about 6,300 km. The Three Gorges Dam on it is the largest power station in the world.

q: Which Chinese city, famous for its riverside Bund and skyline of towers, has the busiest container port in the world?
fact: With nearly 25 million people, it is one of the largest cities on Earth. Its port has topped the world ranking every year since 2010.

q: Which white marble tomb in Agra did Emperor Shah Jahan build for his wife Mumtaz?
fact: It took about 20 years to build, and its marble seems to change color from pink at dawn to gold at sunset.

q: Which bat-and-ball game is by far the most popular sport in India?
fact: The Indian Premier League, started in 2008, is one of the richest sports leagues in the world.

q: What is the highest mountain on Earth, on this country's border with China?
fact: It is 8,849 m high, a figure China and Nepal announced together in 2020.

q: Which spicy fermented cabbage dish is served with almost every Korean meal?
fact: Families often make a whole winter's supply together in autumn - a tradition called kimjang, on UNESCO's heritage list.

q: What is the name of the Korean alphabet, created under King Sejong in the 1440s?
fact: Some of its letters were drawn to show the shape of the mouth and tongue when making each sound.

q: Which sail-shaped luxury hotel in Dubai stands on its own artificial island?
fact: It opened in 1999. Its rooftop helipad, more than 200 m up, has hosted a tennis match and a golf drive.

q: Which ancient city, carved into pink sandstone cliffs, is Jordan's most famous sight?
fact: It was the capital of the Nabataeans more than 2,000 years ago, and was described to Europe by a Swiss traveler in 1812.

q: Which drink is Sri Lanka world-famous for, still often sold under the island's old name, Ceylon?
fact: Coffee was the island's main crop until a plant disease wiped it out in the 1870s, and tea took its place.

q: Which ancient city in southern Iran, begun by Darius I around 518 BC, was the grand ceremonial capital of the Persian kings?
fact: Alexander the Great burned its palaces in 330 BC. Its Greek name means 'city of the Persians'.

q: Which lake on the island of Sumatra is the largest volcanic lake in the world?
fact: It is about 100 km long, and Samosir, the island in its middle, covers about 630 square km - not much smaller than Singapore.

q: What is the round felt tent that is the traditional home of Mongolian herders called in English?
fact: A family can take one down in a few hours and carry it to new pastures on animals or a truck.

q: Which mountain people of Nepal are famous as expert Himalayan climbers and guides?
fact: Tenzing Norgay, who stood on top of Everest with Edmund Hillary in 1953, was a Sherpa.

q: Which Indian independence leader, called 'Mahatma' or 'great soul', led the Salt March of 1930?
fact: His birthday, October 2, is a national holiday in India and the UN's International Day of Non-Violence.

q: Which twin skyscrapers in Kuala Lumpur were the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 to 2004?
fact: Each tower is about 452 m tall, and they are named after Malaysia's national oil company.

q: What were the sword-carrying warriors of old Japan, who served powerful lords, called?
fact: They followed a code of honor later called bushido. Their class was abolished in the 1870s as Japan modernized.

q: Which grandson of Genghis Khan founded China's Yuan dynasty and welcomed Marco Polo to his court?
fact: He built his capital, Khanbaliq, where Beijing stands today.

q: Which religion began in ancient India with the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama?
fact: Siddhartha became known as the Buddha, meaning 'the awakened one'.

q: Which board game, now played worldwide, grew out of an ancient Indian game called chaturanga?
fact: From India it spread to Persia, where 'shah mat' - 'the king is helpless' - gave us the word checkmate.

q: Which festival, marked across East Asia with dragon dances and red envelopes, starts the year by the moon calendar?
fact: It falls between January 21 and February 20. In China it is also called the Spring Festival, and in Vietnam, Tet.

q: Which pale, spotted big cat lives high in the mountains of Central Asia and the Himalayas?
fact: Its thick tail, almost as long as its body, helps it balance on rocks and wraps around it like a scarf in the cold.

q: Which grain is the staple food for most people in Asia?
fact: Asia grows and eats about 90 percent of all the rice in the world.

q: Which river flows north through this country to the Mediterranean Sea?
fact: Almost all Egyptians live in the narrow green strip along its banks and delta - the rest of the country is desert.

q: What is the giant limestone statue with a lion's body and a human head that lies beside the pyramids of Giza?
fact: It was carved out of a single ridge of rock and is about 73 m long.

q: Which boy pharaoh's tomb, packed with gold, was found by Howard Carter in 1922?
fact: His innermost coffin is made of solid gold and weighs about 110 kg.

q: What is the highest mountain in this country and in all of Africa?
fact: At 5,895 m it is the tallest free-standing mountain on Earth, and it has snow on top although it lies close to the equator.

q: Which East African language, spoken by over 100 million people, gave English the word 'safari'?
fact: Safari means 'journey' in it. It is an official language of Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda and Rwanda, and of the African Union.

q: Which flat-topped mountain overlooks Cape Town?
fact: Its flat top is about 3 km wide, and a 'tablecloth' of cloud often pours over its edge.

q: Which South African leader, freed from prison in 1990, became the country's president in 1994?
fact: His birthday, July 18, is marked by the UN every year as Nelson Mandela International Day.

q: Which Moroccan spice blend has a name meaning 'head of the shop' in Arabic?
fact: Each spice seller makes a personal mix, sometimes from more than 20 spices - the best the shop has to offer.

q: Which huge waterfall on the Zambezi River lies on the border of Zambia and Zimbabwe?
fact: Its local name, Mosi-oa-Tunya, means 'the smoke that thunders'.

q: Which spongy sourdough flatbread is eaten with almost every meal in Ethiopia?
fact: It is eaten from a shared tray: pieces are torn off by hand and used to scoop up spicy stews called wat.

q: Which Nigerian author wrote the 1958 novel Things Fall Apart?
fact: It is one of the most widely read African novels, translated into more than 50 languages.

q: Which river delta in this country spreads out into the Kalahari and never reaches the sea?
fact: Its water falls as rain in Angola months earlier. In 2014 it became the 1,000th site on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

q: What is the name of the long plastic horn whose buzz filled the stadiums at the 2010 World Cup in South Africa?
fact: One study measured its blast at 116 decibels from 1 m away - loud enough to harm hearing - and some sports events later banned it.

q: Which large, spiky flower is South Africa's national flower?
fact: The national cricket team is nicknamed the Proteas after it.

q: Which crop, the main ingredient of chocolate, has long been one of Ghana's biggest exports?
fact: A blacksmith named Tetteh Quarshie is credited with bringing cocoa beans to Ghana in the late 1870s.

q: Which Arabic word for 'city' is used for the old walled quarters of Fez, Marrakesh and Tunis?
fact: The old medina of Fez, with thousands of narrow lanes, is one of the largest car-free city areas in the world.

q: Which herding people of Kenya and Tanzania are known for red cloaks and a jumping dance?
fact: Wealth is traditionally counted in cattle. In the jumping dance, called adumu, young men compete to leap highest.

q: Which animal, the tallest on Earth, has just seven neck bones - the same number as humans?
fact: Each of those bones can be more than 25 cm long, and its dark tongue is about 45 cm long.

q: Which African big cat is the fastest land animal on Earth?
fact: It can reach about 100 km/h, but only for a sprint of a few hundred meters.

q: Which mountain range runs across Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia?
fact: Its highest peak, Toubkal in Morocco, reaches 4,167 m and is often snowy in winter.

q: Which tiny steamed grains of semolina are a staple food across North Africa?
fact: In 2020 UNESCO listed its traditions as heritage shared by Algeria, Mauritania, Morocco and Tunisia.

q: Which language is the most widely spoken in North Africa?
fact: Berber (Amazigh) languages are also widely spoken and became official in Morocco in 2011 and Algeria in 2016.

q: What are the West African storytellers called who keep family histories alive in song?
fact: The role passes down through families, and many griots play the kora, a harp-lute with 21 strings.

q: What name is given to the family of 'sowing' board games played with seeds in rows of pits across Africa?
fact: Players scoop up the seeds in one pit and drop them one by one into the next. It is among the oldest games still played.

q: Which vast canyon in Arizona, up to 1.8 km deep, is one of the most famous sights in the US?
fact: Its rock walls show close to two billion years of Earth's history, layer upon layer.

q: Which orange-red suspension bridge spans the entrance to San Francisco Bay?
fact: When it opened in 1937 it was the longest suspension bridge in the world. Its color is called 'International Orange'.

q: What is the name of the yearly championship game of American football, one of the most watched TV events in the US?
fact: The winning team receives the Vince Lombardi Trophy, and the game is usually played in early February.

q: Which American inventor patented the phonograph in 1878 and set up a famous lab at Menlo Park?
fact: He held more than 1,000 US patents, from light bulbs to film cameras.

q: Which tree's leaf is shown on the flag of Canada?
fact: The red-and-white maple leaf flag was first raised on February 15, 1965.

q: Which Mexican dip is made from mashed avocado?
fact: The Aztecs were already making it. The name comes from the Nahuatl for 'avocado sauce'.

q: Which Mexican painter, famous for her self-portraits, lived in the 'Blue House' in Mexico City?
fact: About a third of her paintings are self-portraits. The Blue House, where she was born, is now a museum about her.

q: Which famous beach in Rio de Janeiro has a promenade paved in a black-and-white wave pattern?
fact: The wave pattern copies the paving of the Rossio square in Lisbon, Portugal.

q: Which vast rainforest covers much of the north of this country?
fact: It spreads across nine countries and is home to roughly one in ten of all known species.

q: What are the giant ancient drawings scratched into the desert of southern Peru called?
fact: Some figures, like a hummingbird and a monkey, are so large that they are best seen from the air.

q: Which high lake does this country share with Peru?
fact: It lies about 3,800 m up. On the Peruvian side, the Uros people live on floating islands made of reeds.

q: Which waterfall in Venezuela is the highest in the world?
fact: Its water drops 979 m. It is named after the US pilot Jimmie Angel, who flew over it in the 1930s.

q: Which bay between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia in Canada has the highest tides in the world?
fact: The water can rise and fall by about 16 m - roughly the height of a five-story building.

q: Which Cuban cocktail is made with white rum, lime, sugar, fresh mint and soda water?
fact: Cuba's other famous rum drink, the daiquiri, is named after a beach near Santiago de Cuba.

q: Which Jamaican singer, leader of the Wailers, recorded 'One Love' and 'No Woman, No Cry'?
fact: His greatest-hits album Legend, released in 1984, is one of the best-selling reggae albums ever.

q: What were the knotted strings the Inca used to keep records called?
fact: The type, color and position of each knot stored numbers - and maybe more. Nobody has fully cracked them yet.

q: Which Arctic people of Canada, Alaska and Greenland traditionally built snow houses on winter hunting trips?
fact: Igloo simply means 'house' in Inuktitut, their language - it does not have to be made of snow.

q: Which remote Pacific island belonging to this country is famous for its giant stone heads, the moai?
fact: There are nearly 1,000 moai, carved from volcanic rock by the island's Rapa Nui people.

q: What is the name of the world's largest salt flat, in southwest Bolivia?
fact: It covers more than 10,000 square km, and after rain it turns into a giant mirror reflecting the sky.

q: Which civilization built the temple cities of Tikal and Palenque in Guatemala and Mexico?
fact: Millions of Maya people still live in Mexico and Central America today, and many speak Mayan languages.

q: Which crop, first grown in Mexico about 9,000 years ago, is now the most produced grain in the world?
fact: Much of the world's harvest feeds farm animals or becomes fuel and syrup, not food eaten straight from the cob.

q: Which hot pepper, first grown in the Americas, now gives much of the heat to Thai and Indian cooking?
fact: It only reached Asia in the 1500s, carried by Portuguese traders. Before that, the heat came from black pepper.

q: Which Italian-born explorer reached the Caribbean in 1492 while sailing for Spain?
fact: He crossed the Atlantic with three ships: the Nina, the Pinta and the Santa Maria.

q: Which leader, born in Caracas, is called 'El Libertador' for freeing much of South America from Spanish rule?
fact: Born in 1783, he led independence campaigns across lands that are now six countries.

q: What name is given to the five huge connected lakes of North America, mostly along the US-Canada border?
fact: Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario together hold about a fifth of the world's fresh surface water.

q: Which huge red sandstone rock in central Australia is sacred to the Anangu people?
fact: It rises about 348 m above the plain. Climbing it has been banned since 2019 out of respect for its traditional owners.

q: What is the name of the world's largest coral reef system, off the coast of Queensland?
fact: It is made of nearly 3,000 separate reefs and stretches more than 2,300 km.

q: Which burrowing Australian marsupial is famous for its cube-shaped droppings?
fact: Its pouch faces backward, so no dirt gets in while it digs.

q: Which harborside building with sail-shaped roofs is Sydney's most famous landmark?
fact: The Danish architect Jorn Utzon won the design competition in 1957, and it opened in 1973.

q: Which lakeside town on New Zealand's South Island calls itself the adventure capital of the world?
fact: The world's first commercial bungee jump opened nearby, at the Kawarau Bridge, in 1988.

q: Which steep, cone-shaped New Zealand volcano, digitally made taller, played Mount Doom in The Lord of the Rings films?
fact: It lies in Tongariro, New Zealand's oldest national park. Close-up Mordor scenes were filmed on the slopes of nearby Mount Ruapehu.

q: Which New Zealander was one of the first two people to reach the top of Everest, in 1953?
fact: He climbed with Tenzing Norgay, and his face is on New Zealand's five-dollar note.

q: In which sport did Fiji win its first Olympic gold medals, at the 2016 and Tokyo 2020 Games?
fact: The 2016 gold was Fiji's first Olympic medal of any color. The women's team took bronze in Tokyo, and the men silver in Paris in 2024.

q: What is the name of the pidgin language spoken across Vanuatu as a common tongue?
fact: Most of its words come from English: 'tangkyu tumas' means 'thank you very much'.

q: Which strait separates mainland Australia from the island of Tasmania?
fact: It is named after George Bass, a ship's doctor who sailed through it with Matthew Flinders in 1798.

q: Which Dutch explorer became the first European to reach Tasmania and New Zealand, in 1642?
fact: The Tasman Sea between Australia and New Zealand is named after him.

q: Which great triangle of Pacific islands, with Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island at its corners, has a Greek name meaning 'many islands'?
fact: Polynesian navigators settled it by canoe, steering by the stars, waves and birds over thousands of kilometers.

q: What is the Maori name for the traditional earth oven, in which food is steamed on hot stones underground?
fact: Food in baskets is covered with cloth and earth and left for hours. In Samoa and Tonga a similar oven is called an umu.

q: On which continent was the coldest temperature ever measured on Earth's surface recorded?
fact: It was -89.2 C, measured at Russia's Vostok research station in 1983.

q: Which international sports event has five interlocking rings as its symbol?
fact: Pierre de Coubertin drew them in 1913 for the five parts of the world. He said their colors, with the white background, appeared on every flag of the time.

q: Which football tournament between national teams is held every four years by FIFA?
fact: The 2026 tournament in the US, Canada and Mexico was the first with 48 teams.

q: Counting both native and second-language speakers, which language is spoken by the most people in the world?
fact: Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers, but English leads once learners are counted.

q: Which is the largest and deepest ocean on Earth?
fact: It covers about a third of Earth's surface - more than all the land put together.

q: Which calendar, introduced in 1582 and named after a pope, is used by most of the world today?
fact: To fix the drift of the old calendar, ten days were skipped: Thursday, October 4, 1582 was followed by Friday, October 15.

q: What is the largest animal known to have ever lived?
fact: It can reach about 30 m long, and a newborn calf already weighs more than 2 tonnes.

q: What is the line of 0 degrees longitude, which passes through Greenwich in London, called?
fact: It was chosen as the world's starting line for longitude and time at a conference in Washington in 1884.

q: What is the imaginary line in the Pacific, near 180 degrees longitude, where the calendar date changes?
fact: It zigzags around island nations such as Kiribati so that no country is split between two dates.
